title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces the rate of unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used the declared model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic netops validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms); the guarded arm could request up to one validator‑triggered repair. We ran N = 240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline: 240/240 safe; guarded: 240/240 safe). The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics the paired contrast can only arise if the single shared initial candidate fails deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied; in this run all shared candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired outcome. We report the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, statistical mapping, and an evidence‑based failure analysis with concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating intent‑driven network configuration is central to modern NetOps. Large language models (LLMs) can produce device configuration sequences from high‑level operator intents, but textual fidelity alone does not guarantee safe application: ordering, transient invariants, protected resources, and cross‑device dependencies matter for semantic safety. Closed‑loop, emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are applied to device images or simulators and deterministically scored—exposes execution and planning failures that text‑only tests miss. A common mitigation pattern is generate–validate–repair (GVR): an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic validator checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations are detected.

We preregistered a paired experiment to measure the causal effect of inserting a deterministic verifier (and permitted repair) into an LLM‑based configuration pipeline. The primary estimand is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded minus baseline) over N paired tasks. The run obeyed a shared_initial_candidate contract: exactly one initial LLM generation was produced per task and reused by both arms; the guarded arm could invoke at most one validator‑triggered repair. This contract makes the causal contrast mechanistically dependent on whether the shared candidate fails validation or whether a repair is applied. Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation executed to completion; (2) an artifact‑grounded reporting of the primary estimand and its exact statistical outputs; and (3) a failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR studies.
sections.related_work:
Recent work advocates executable, emulation‑grounded benchmarks to evaluate LLM agents on NetOps workflows rather than only on text fidelity; such benchmarks reveal planning and execution faults [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents GVR‑style patterns and shows that deterministic validators often enable high repair coverage for many fault classes, though semantic coverage depends on verifier design [2],[3]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, and verifier integration as promising safety patterns for NetOps automation while noting open questions about external validity and verifier scalability [4],[5]. Engineering precedents from configuration analysis tools (e.g., Batfish) demonstrate value in incremental and localized verification for network changes [6].

Our study differs from prior work by (a) preregistering a precise paired estimand, (b) executing under shared_initial_candidate semantics where a single generation is reused across arms, (c) using closed‑loop emulator scoring to define semantic safety, and (d) archiving per‑call traces and validator traces so that the measured estimand is directly traceable to the recorded artifacts.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: We preregistered the study (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline) where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The preregistration fixed design, task composition, analysis plan, retry policy, and exclusion rules prior to observing outcomes.

Design and task corpus: The experiment used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: for each of N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks the system produced exactly one initial LLM generation which was reused by both conditions (baseline LLM‑only and guarded GVR). Task composition: in‑distribution = 144, distribution‑shift = 48, adversarial‑prompt = 48. Tasks were deterministic draws from a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus designed to exercise ordering, dependency, and protected‑resource constraints.

Model, verifier, and adapter contract: Execution used the declared hosted model gpt-5-mini and a deterministic netops validator. Under the shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm may only differ from baseline if the single shared candidate fails deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair is applied; the guarded arm was allowed up to one repair attempt per task. The preregistered retry policy permitted limited infra retries for technical failures; such retries did not alter scientific pairing decisions.

Scoring and statistical analysis: Final outcomes were binary (safe vs unsafe) determined by emulator execution and semantic invariant checks. The prespecified primary analysis used a paired‑binary estimator producing a contingency table of paired outcomes, an exact McNemar two‑sided test on discordant pairs, and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval. Bootstrap parameters were 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729 as preregistered. Predeclared sensitivity analyses covered potential 'possible false‑safe' flags (validator PASS but emulator unsafe) and infra failures; those channels were exercised if flagged.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed as preregistered. Planned episodes = 480 (two episodes per task); completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Exactly one initial LLM generation per task was produced and reused across arms, consistent with the shared_initial_candidate contract. No infra failures or preregistration exclusions occurred.

Primary outcomes and contingency: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Aggregate counts: baseline safe = 240, baseline unsafe = 0; guarded safe = 240, guarded unsafe = 0. Paired contingency: n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 (guarded safe, baseline unsafe) = 0; n01 (guarded unsafe, baseline safe) = 0; n00 (both unsafe) = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. The paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs were applied in any guarded episode. Representative validator traces recorded validation metadata (difficulty labels, observed touched fields, and PASS semantics) for all tasks; because every shared candidate passed deterministic validation, the guarded arm had no opportunity to alter a final configuration relative to baseline under the preregistered contract.

Planned sensitivities unused: The preregistered sensitivity channels for 'possible false‑safe' flags and infra failures were not exercised because no such flags or failures were observed; subgroup contrasts (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial) are degenerate here (all subgroups show zero unsafe applies for both arms).
sections.discussion:
Mechanistic explanation of the null paired contrast: Under shared_initial_candidate semantics both arms begin from the identical LLM candidate for each task; therefore, by design, a paired divergence can only occur if the shared candidate fails deterministic validation and the guarded pipeline applies a repair that changes the final configuration. In this run, all shared candidates passed validation and no repairs were invoked; this mechanistic fact fully explains the degenerate paired contingency (estimate = 0.0, CI = [0.0,0.0], p = 1.0).

Design tradeoffs and implications: The shared_initial_candidate contract reduces model‑call budget and ensures a strict pairing of generator outputs, which simplifies causal attribution when the shared generation fails. However, it also prevents generator variability between arms and therefore makes demonstration of verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures. To measure verifier effectiveness as a causal intervention in practice, experimenters should consider at least one of: (A) allowing independent initial generations per arm so the verifier can be tested against generator variability; (B) increasing adversary strength or coverage to create more candidate failures; or (C) expanding the repair budget (multiple iterative repairs) to exercise repair search dynamics.

Threats to validity and scope: Internal validity is constrained by the preregistered generation semantics (shared_initial_candidate) and by the finite coverage of the deterministic validator; construct validity depends on whether the validator's check-set captures the operationally relevant semantic faults; external validity is limited by the synthetic emulation corpus and single hosted model evaluated. These limitations are material for interpreting the null paired outcome and guide the recommendations below.

Recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations (artifact‑grounded): (1) If the goal is a nondegenerate paired causal contrast, avoid reusing a single shared candidate across arms or intentionally inject generator variability for one arm. (2) Increase repair iterations and instrument repair traces to study repair effectiveness and search behavior. (3) Strengthen adversarial prompt procedures (beyond a single fixed seed) to probe adaptive manipulations. (4) Expand verifier semantic coverage and include automated cross‑checks between validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect potential false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, emulation‑grounded paired evaluation of a GVR pipeline using a declared hosted LLM and a deterministic netops validator under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Observed result: every paired episode was safe under both arms, producing a degenerate paired contrast (difference = 0.00; 95% CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). This outcome is fully explained by the preregistered generation semantics: because a single initial generation was reused across arms and all shared candidates passed deterministic validation, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to alter final outcomes. The archived execution and analysis artifacts support these conclusions and point to specific design changes (independent generation semantics, larger repair budgets, stronger adversaries, and broader verifier coverage) that are necessary for future informative demonstrations of verifier benefit in LLM‑based NetOps pipelines.

limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a synthetic, emulation‑grounded corpus; external validity to production multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: only the declared hosted model (gpt-5-mini) was evaluated; results do not imply generality across other models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design reused a single initial generation per task, which prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts followed a preregistered fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: the deterministic validator implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected.
